narrative.text: Vyktor sets a framed portrait on your desk. It is the standard issue—glass front, oak frame, the same photograph that has hung in every post office, school, and ministry for thirty years. The face staring out is Chancellor Halvek.
Eleven thousand. That is the latest count from the Interior Ministry. The civil servants are waiting for an order. They are afraid to take them down without one, and they are afraid to leave them up.

Eleven thousand faces of the man who dissolved the parliament, who built the BNI, who took my father in the night. They stare down from the walls of the very offices meant to serve the people he imprisoned. The clerks are right to be afraid. This is not a question of interior decorating. It is the first test of whether this government intends to erase the past or simply ignore it.

choices.text: Remove them. By the end of the week. Let the people see the walls are bare. The era of Halvek is over.
Box them. Catalog them. Send them to the National Archive. The walls will simply change, quietly. We do not need a spectacle.
Leave them. The Republic has bigger problems than pictures. Let the transition speak for itself.

narrative.text: Vyktor nods. By Friday, the walls are bare. The dust outlines remain, a ghostly reminder of where the regime used to watch.
The morning editions are already printing. The Herald is calling it a 'purge of national memory'. Vael's editorial board worked through the night.

Vael's papers frame our break from tyranny as an act of vandalism. He doesn't need to attack me directly; he just shapes how the country sees the empty walls. The narrative is already slipping out of my hands.

choices.text: Let them write what they want. The walls are bare.

narrative.text: Vyktor issues the memo. Over the next two weeks, the portraits disappear quietly into boxes, sent to a warehouse in the suburbs. No announcement is made.
Curiously, the Standard ran a piece today praising your 'mature restraint'. Lucan Vael apparently finds your approach... reasonable.

Praise from Lucan Vael is more dangerous than criticism. It means he believes I can be managed. It means he thinks restraint is just another word for fear. By avoiding a spectacle, I may have simply handed him the narrative.

choices.text: Reasonable is better than war. For now.

narrative.text: The portraits stay. The civil servants sigh, perhaps in relief, perhaps in disappointment. The face of Halvek continues to stare down from the walls of the Republic.
The reformists are unhappy. They expected a clean break. But Vael's papers haven't attacked you, which is something.

The reformists see compromise; Vael sees weakness. I have kept the peace, but the ghost of the old regime still haunts the halls. Perhaps it always will. Let them look at his face and remember what we are rebuilding from.

choices.text: We have bigger battles to fight. Let the pictures hang.
